title: Who can opt for the GST composition scheme
text: The composition scheme under section 10 of the CGST Act is a simple, low-rate option for small businesses. A registered person whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year did not exceed Rs 1.5 crore can opt for it (Notification 14/2019-Central Tax, from 1 April 2019); the limit is Rs 75 lakh in Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura and Uttarakhand. It is meant for traders, manufacturers and restaurants. A person cannot opt if he supplies goods or services not leviable to GST, makes inter-state outward supplies, is a casual or non-resident taxable person, or manufactures notified goods such as ice cream, pan masala and tobacco. If several registrations share one PAN, all must opt together. The option lapses on the day turnover crosses the limit during the year.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 10 (Composition levy); CGST Rules 7 and 62; Notification 14/2019-CT; Notification 36/2023-CT
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Composition scheme tax rates for traders, manufacturers and restaurants
text: Rule 7 of the CGST Rules prescribes composition rates as a percentage of turnover in the state; each rate is charged once as CGST and once as SGST, so the total is double the rule's figure. Manufacturers (other than of notified goods) pay 0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST = 1% of turnover. Restaurants and other suppliers of food or drink served as a service (paragraph 6(b) of Schedule II) pay 2.5% + 2.5% = 5%. Traders and other eligible suppliers pay 0.5% + 0.5% = 1% of the turnover of taxable supplies, so exempt sales like fresh vegetables are excluded. These rates were not changed by GST 2.0 in September 2025. Composition dealers pay this tax from their own pocket; they cannot collect it from customers.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 10 (Composition levy); CGST Rules 7 and 62; Notification 14/2019-CT; Notification 36/2023-CT
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Restrictions on composition dealers: no ITC, no tax collection, bill of supply
text: A composition dealer cannot collect any tax from customers and cannot claim input tax credit on purchases (section 10(4)). Instead of a tax invoice, he issues a bill of supply, which must mention "composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies"; he must also display this on his signboard. He cannot make inter-state outward supplies, so a composition shopkeeper in Pune cannot sell to a buyer in Gujarat. He can sell goods within his own state through an e-commerce operator that collects TCS (allowed from 1 October 2023 under Notification 36/2023-CT), but cannot supply services through e-commerce operators. A goods trader or manufacturer under composition may also supply services (other than restaurant services) up to 10% of the previous year's state turnover or Rs 5 lakh, whichever is higher.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 10 (Composition levy); CGST Rules 7 and 62; Notification 14/2019-CT; Notification 36/2023-CT
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Composition scheme for service providers (6% scheme under section 10(2A))
text: Service providers and mixed suppliers who are not eligible for the regular composition scheme can opt for a separate scheme under section 10(2A) of the CGST Act (first introduced by Notification 2/2019-Central Tax (Rate) from 1 April 2019). The condition is that aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year did not exceed Rs 50 lakh. Tax is paid at 3% CGST + 3% SGST, i.e. 6% of the turnover of supplies in the state (rule 7). As with regular composition, the person cannot make inter-state outward supplies, cannot supply services through e-commerce operators that collect TCS, cannot make non-taxable supplies, cannot collect tax from customers, and cannot claim input tax credit. A local freelancer or tutor with only in-state clients and turnover under Rs 50 lakh may consider this scheme.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 10 (Composition levy); CGST Rules 7 and 62; Notification 14/2019-CT; Notification 36/2023-CT
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Composition scheme forms and due dates (CMP-02, CMP-08, GSTR-4)
text: To opt into composition for a financial year, an existing registered person files intimation in Form GST CMP-02 on the GST portal before the start of that year; a new applicant can choose composition in the registration application. A composition taxpayer then has two filings under rule 62: Form GST CMP-08, a quarterly statement-cum-challan for paying self-assessed tax, due by the 18th of the month after each quarter (for example, 18 October for July to September); and Form GSTR-4, the annual return. From FY 2024-25 onwards, GSTR-4 is due by 30 June following the end of the financial year (earlier it was 30 April). Tax in CMP-08 must be paid in cash from the electronic cash ledger. Composition dealers do not file the monthly GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B returns that regular taxpayers file.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 10 (Composition levy); CGST Rules 7 and 62; Notification 14/2019-CT; Notification 36/2023-CT
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Mandatory details on a GST tax invoice
text: A registered person making a taxable supply must issue a tax invoice under section 31 of the CGST Act. Rule 46 lists what it must contain: name, address and GSTIN of the supplier; a consecutive serial number of up to 16 characters, unique for the financial year; date of issue; name, address and GSTIN of the recipient if registered; for unregistered buyers, name, delivery address and state when the value is Rs 50,000 or more; HSN code of goods or SAC of services; description; quantity and unit; total and taxable value after discount; GST rate and amount split into CGST, SGST/UTGST, IGST and cess; place of supply with state name for inter-state supplies; whether tax is payable on reverse charge; and the signature or digital signature of the supplier. E-invoices must also carry a QR code with the IRN.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 31; CGST Rules 46, 48(4), 49; Notification 78/2020-CT (HSN digits); Notification 10/2023-CT (e-invoice threshold)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Bill of supply instead of a tax invoice
text: A registered person who supplies exempt goods or services, or who has opted for the composition scheme, cannot charge GST and must issue a bill of supply instead of a tax invoice (section 31(3)(c) and rule 49). A bill of supply contains the supplier's name, address and GSTIN, a consecutive serial number unique for the financial year, date of issue, recipient details if registered, HSN or SAC code, description, value of the supply after discount, and the supplier's signature. It shows no tax amount. A composition dealer must also write "composition taxable person, not eligible to collect tax on supplies" on top of the bill. A small kirana under composition therefore gives customers a bill of supply, not a GST invoice.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 31; CGST Rules 46, 48(4), 49; Notification 78/2020-CT (HSN digits); Notification 10/2023-CT (e-invoice threshold)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: How many HSN or SAC digits must be shown on invoices
text: From 1 April 2021, Notification 78/2020-Central Tax fixed the number of HSN (goods) or SAC (services) digits on tax invoices by aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year. Taxpayers with turnover up to Rs 5 crore must show at least a 4-digit code, and those above Rs 5 crore must show 6 digits. A taxpayer with turnover up to Rs 5 crore may omit the HSN code on invoices issued to unregistered (B2C) customers, but must show 4 digits on B2B invoices. HSN-wise summaries are also reported in Table 12 of GSTR-1.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 31; CGST Rules 46, 48(4), 49; Notification 78/2020-CT (HSN digits); Notification 10/2023-CT (e-invoice threshold)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: E-invoicing threshold: aggregate turnover above Rs 5 crore
text: E-invoicing means reporting each B2B invoice to the government's Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), which returns an Invoice Reference Number (IRN) and a signed QR code that must be printed on the invoice (rule 48(4)). From 1 August 2023, Notification 10/2023-Central Tax made e-invoicing mandatory for registered persons whose aggregate turnover in any financial year from 2017-18 onwards exceeded Rs 5 crore (the limit had been stepped down from Rs 500 crore in 2020 to Rs 10 crore by October 2022). It applies to B2B supplies, exports and credit and debit notes, not to sales to ordinary consumers. A business above the threshold that issues a B2B invoice without an IRN has not issued a valid invoice, and the buyer may lose input tax credit. A small shop below Rs 5 crore does not need e-invoicing.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Section 31; CGST Rules 46, 48(4), 49; Notification 78/2020-CT (HSN digits); Notification 10/2023-CT (e-invoice threshold)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Basic conditions for claiming input tax credit
text: Input tax credit (ITC) lets a registered person reduce output GST by the GST paid on purchases used in business (section 16(1) of the CGST Act). Under section 16(2), ITC is allowed only if the buyer has a tax invoice or debit note from a registered supplier; the supplier has reported it in GSTR-1 and it appears in the buyer's GSTR-2B; the goods or services have actually been received; the supplier has paid the tax to the government; and the buyer has filed GSTR-3B. If the buyer does not pay the supplier within 180 days of the invoice date, the ITC must be reversed with interest, and can be reclaimed once paid. Under section 16(4), ITC for a financial year must be claimed by 30 November of the following year or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 16 and 17(5) (input tax credit)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Blocked credits under section 17(5) and no ITC for composition dealers
text: Section 17(5) of the CGST Act blocks ITC on certain items even if used in business. Examples: motor vehicles for carrying up to 13 persons, including the driver, unless the business supplies such vehicles, transports passengers or runs a driving school, plus their insurance and repairs; food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services and cosmetic surgery; life and health insurance; club and gym memberships; travel benefits for employees on leave; goods or services for construction of immovable property on own account; goods lost, stolen, destroyed or given as free samples or gifts; and tax paid under composition. So a freelancer cannot claim GST paid on a personal car or on restaurant meals. A composition dealer cannot claim any ITC at all (section 10(4)), and services taxed at 5% without ITC, such as salons and budget hotels, cannot use credit against that tax.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 16 and 17(5) (input tax credit)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: GST on ACs, TVs, dishwashers, fridges and washing machines before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, air-conditioners (HSN 8415) and dishwashing machines (HSN 8422) were taxed at 28% GST. Television sets and monitors larger than 32 inches were also at 28%, while TVs and monitors up to 32 inches were at 18%. Refrigerators and washing machines were not in the 28% slab during this period: they had already been cut from 28% to 18% from 27 July 2018. So an AC bought in August 2025 carried 28% GST, a 43-inch LED TV 28%, and a refrigerator or washing machine 18%. These are the old, pre-GST 2.0 rates and apply to sales up to 21 September 2025.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on ACs, TVs, dishwashers, fridges and washing machines from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025 under GST 2.0, air-conditioning machines and dishwashing machines moved from 28% to 18% GST. All television sets, including LCD and LED TVs, and monitors and projectors are now uniformly taxed at 18%, whatever the screen size; earlier only TVs up to 32 inches were at 18%. Refrigerators and washing machines remain at 18%; GST 2.0 did not change their rate because they were already at 18%. So today an AC, a 55-inch TV, a dishwasher, a fridge or a washing machine all attract 18% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on small cars, motorcycles and three-wheelers before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, all motor cars, motorcycles (of any engine size) and three-wheelers were taxed at 28% GST. Cars and bigger motorcycles also attracted compensation cess on top of GST, which varied with engine size, length and fuel type, so the total tax on a mid-size or large car or SUV was well above 28%. Buses, goods trucks, ambulances and many auto parts were also at 28%. These rates apply to vehicles bought up to 21 September 2025, for example a motorcycle bought in July 2025.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on small cars, motorcycles and three-wheelers from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, small cars moved from 28% to 18% GST. A small car means a petrol, LPG or CNG car with engine capacity up to 1200cc and length up to 4000 mm, or a diesel car up to 1500cc and 4000 mm. Motorcycles, scooters and mopeds up to 350cc, three-wheelers, buses, trucks and ambulances also moved from 28% to 18%, and all auto parts are uniformly at 18%. Mid-size and large cars (above these limits), SUVs above 1500cc with length over 4000 mm and ground clearance of 170 mm or more, and motorcycles above 350cc are taxed at 40%, with no compensation cess on top.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on cement before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, Portland cement, aluminous cement, slag cement and similar hydraulic cements (HSN 2523), including clinkers, were taxed at 28% GST, the highest regular slab. A builder, contractor or individual buying cement bags for house construction during this period paid 28% GST on the bill. A hardware or building-material shop selling cement had to charge 28% on such sales made up to 21 September 2025.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on cement from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, the GST Council reduced GST on cement (HSN 2523: Portland, aluminous, slag, super-sulphate and similar hydraulic cements, including clinkers) from 28% to 18%. This was one of the headline changes of GST 2.0 meant to reduce construction and housing costs. A building-material dealer selling cement today must charge 18% GST, and a registered buyer using it in business can claim input tax credit at 18%, subject to the normal ITC rules.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on hair oil, soap, shampoo and toothpaste before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, everyday personal-care products were mostly taxed at 18% GST. This covered hair oil and shampoo (HSN 3305), toothpaste and dental floss (HSN 3306), toilet soap bars (HSN 3401), talcum and face powder (HSN 3304), and shaving cream and aftershave (HSN 3307). Tooth powder was taxed at 12%. A kirana or general store selling a bottle of hair oil or a tube of toothpaste in this period charged 18% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on hair oil, soap, shampoo and toothpaste from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, GST on common personal-care items was cut to 5%. Hair oil, shampoo, toothpaste, dental floss, toilet soap bars, talcum and face powder and shaving cream and aftershave moved from 18% to 5%, tooth powder moved from 12% to 5%, and toothbrushes are also at 5%. Bicycles, tableware, kitchenware and many household articles also moved to 5%. So toothpaste, soap and shampoo are no longer at 18%; a shop selling them today should charge 5% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on butter, ghee, cheese and packaged food before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, butter, ghee, butter oil and dairy spreads (HSN 0405), cheese (HSN 0406), condensed milk and pre-packaged namkeen and bhujia were taxed at 12% GST. Chocolates, biscuits, pastries and cakes, cornflakes, ice cream, sauces, instant noodles, coffee extracts and many other packaged foods were at 18%. UHT milk and pre-packaged, labelled paneer were at 5%, and paratha and similar Indian breads at 18%. These old rates apply to sales made up to 21 September 2025.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on butter, ghee, cheese and packaged food from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, butter, ghee, cheese, condensed milk and pre-packaged namkeen and bhujia moved from 12% to 5% GST. Chocolates, biscuits, cakes, ice cream, cornflakes, pasta, instant noodles, sauces, soups and coffee moved from 18% to 5%. UHT milk and pre-packaged, labelled paneer (chena) became nil-rated (from 5%), and all Indian breads such as roti, chapati, paratha and parotta are now nil. A dairy or sweet shop selling packaged ghee or cheese today charges 5% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on life and health insurance premiums before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, individual life insurance and individual health insurance premiums were taxed at 18% GST as financial services (SAC heading 9971), with input tax credit available to the insurer. A freelancer paying a Rs 20,000 health insurance premium for a family floater policy in this period would have paid about Rs 3,600 as GST on top, i.e. 18%.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on life and health insurance premiums from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, GST on all individual life insurance policies, whether term, ULIP or endowment, and on all individual health insurance policies, including family floater and senior-citizen policies, was exempted (18% to nil). Reinsurance of these policies is also exempt. So an individual buying a term plan or a personal health policy pays no GST on the premium today. The exemption is for individual policies; group policies taken by employers are not covered by this change.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on aerated drinks, luxury cars and gaming before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, aerated waters and other drinks containing added sugar or flavouring, caffeinated beverages and carbonated fruit drinks were taxed at 28% GST plus compensation cess. Mid-size and large cars, SUVs and motorcycles above 350cc were taxed at 28% GST plus compensation cess. Betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery and online money gaming were taxed at 28%, as was admission to casinos, race clubs and sporting events like the IPL. Personal aircraft and yachts were also at 28% plus cess.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: The 40% de-merit rate from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, a special 40% GST rate applies to a short list of sin and luxury items, with no compensation cess on top. It covers aerated waters and all drinks with added sugar or flavouring, caffeinated beverages and carbonated fruit drinks (28% to 40%); mid-size and large cars and SUVs, motorcycles above 350cc, personal aircraft and yachts (28% to 40%); and betting, casinos, gambling, horse racing, lottery and online money gaming, plus admission to casinos, race clubs and sporting events like the IPL (28% to 40%). Pan masala and tobacco moved to 40% only from 1 February 2026. Plain unsweetened mineral water moved from 18% to 5%.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on clothes and footwear before 22 September 2025
text: Before GST 2.0, the price cut-off for clothes and footwear was Rs 1,000. Readymade garments and clothing accessories with a sale value up to Rs 1,000 per piece were taxed at 5%, and those above Rs 1,000 at 12%. Footwear up to Rs 1,000 per pair was taxed at 12% (raised from 5% with effect from 1 January 2022), and footwear above Rs 1,000 per pair at 18%. A cloth shop selling a Rs 1,800 kurta in August 2025 therefore charged 12% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on clothes and footwear from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, the cut-off for clothes and footwear is Rs 2,500. Apparel, clothing accessories and made-up textile articles with a sale value up to Rs 2,500 per piece are taxed at 5%; above Rs 2,500 per piece they are taxed at 18% (up from 12%). Footwear with a sale value up to Rs 2,500 per pair is taxed at 5% (down from 12%), and footwear above Rs 2,500 per pair stays at 18%. So a Rs 1,800 kurta is at 5% today, but a Rs 3,000 jacket is at 18%.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on hotel rooms, salons and gyms before 22 September 2025
text: Up to 21 September 2025, hotel accommodation with a value up to Rs 7,500 per unit per day was taxed at 12% GST with input tax credit; rooms above Rs 7,500 were at 18%. Beauty and physical well-being services, including salons, barbers, beauty parlours, gyms, health clubs, fitness centres and yoga centres, were taxed at 18% with input tax credit. A salon owner billing a customer in August 2025 therefore charged 18% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on hotel rooms, salons and gyms from 22 September 2025
text: From 22 September 2025, hotel accommodation valued up to Rs 7,500 per unit per day is taxed at 5% without input tax credit (earlier 12%); rooms above Rs 7,500 stay at 18%. Beauty and physical well-being services, including salons, barbers, gyms, health clubs, fitness centres and yoga centres, are taxed at 5% without input tax credit (earlier 18%). "Without ITC" means the salon, gym or hotel cannot claim credit of GST paid on its own purchases against this 5% output tax. Movie tickets up to Rs 100 moved from 12% to 5%.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council, Annexures I-IV (HSN-wise "From"/"To" rate tables) and PIB FAQs on the 56th GST Council decisions
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST rate slabs before GST 2.0 (1 July 2017 to 21 September 2025)
text: From the launch of GST on 1 July 2017 until 21 September 2025, goods and services were taxed under a four-tier structure of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, with nil-rated and exempt items below it. The 28% slab covered items such as air-conditioners, cement, cars and motorcycles, large TVs and aerated drinks. On top of GST, a separate GST compensation cess was charged on many 28% goods, for example cars, aerated drinks, pan masala and tobacco. The 12% slab covered items such as butter, ghee, cheese, namkeen and most hotel rooms up to Rs 7,500 a night, while the 18% slab covered most services and many FMCG goods like soap, shampoo and toothpaste. GST is levied under section 9 of the CGST Act at the rate notified by the government. Use this chunk for any question about a period up to 21 September 2025, for example "GST rate in August 2025" or "FY 2024-25".
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB press release, 3 Sep 2025) and FAQs on the decisions of the 56th GST Council
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST 2.0: new two-slab structure from 22 September 2025
text: The 56th GST Council meeting, held in New Delhi on 3 September 2025 under Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, approved the "next-generation GST reforms", popularly called GST 2.0. The old four-tier structure was rationalised into two main rates: a merit rate of 5% and a standard rate of 18%, plus a special de-merit rate of 40% for a small list of sin and luxury goods and services. The 12% and 28% slabs were largely removed: most 12% items moved to 5% and most 28% items moved to 18%. Some items became nil, such as UHT milk, pre-packaged paneer, Indian breads like roti and paratha, and individual life and health insurance. The new rates on services and on all goods except tobacco products and pan masala apply from 22 September 2025. The Council's FAQ confirms that the GST registration threshold did not change as part of this reform.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB press release, 3 Sep 2025) and FAQs on the decisions of the 56th GST Council
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST compensation cess: what happened after GST 2.0
text: GST compensation cess was an extra levy, over and above GST, on luxury and demerit goods such as cars, aerated drinks, tobacco and pan masala. Under GST 2.0, the Council decided to end the compensation cess levy and to fold its effect into the new 40% rate. From 22 September 2025, cars, motorcycles above 350cc and sugary or caffeinated drinks no longer carry compensation cess; they pay GST alone (18% or 40%). For pan masala, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, unmanufactured tobacco and bidi, the old GST rate plus cess continued until the cess loans were repaid. From 1 February 2026 the compensation cess on these tobacco goods was made nil, and they moved to the new GST rates. Pan masala now also attracts a separate Health Security se National Security (HSNS) Cess and tobacco products an additional central excise duty, both outside GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB press release, 3 Sep 2025) and FAQs on the decisions of the 56th GST Council
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on pan masala, cigarettes and tobacco up to 31 January 2026
text: Pan masala, gutkha, cigarettes, chewing tobacco such as zarda, unmanufactured tobacco and bidi were kept outside the 22 September 2025 rate change. The 56th GST Council decided that these goods would continue at their existing rates of GST and compensation cess until the loans and interest under the compensation cess account were fully repaid. So for any period up to 31 January 2026, pan masala, cigarettes and tobacco products were taxed at 28% GST plus the applicable compensation cess, and bidi at 28%. A shop selling cigarettes or pan masala in, say, October 2025 therefore still charged 28% GST plus cess, even though most other goods had already moved to GST 2.0 rates.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB press release, 3 Sep 2025) and FAQs on the decisions of the 56th GST Council
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST on pan masala, cigarettes and tobacco from 1 February 2026
text: From 1 February 2026 the deferred GST 2.0 rates for tobacco goods came into force. Pan masala, gutkha, cigarettes, chewing tobacco and other manufactured tobacco and unmanufactured tobacco are taxed at the 40% de-merit rate, while bidi is taxed at 18%. GST on these goods is computed on the declared retail sale price (RSP) instead of transaction value. The GST compensation cess on these goods was reduced to nil from the same date. In place of the cess, pan masala manufacturers pay a capacity-based Health Security se National Security (HSNS) Cess, and cigarettes and other tobacco products pay an additional central excise duty; both are outside GST and are charged over and above the 40% GST.
source_title: Recommendations of the 56th Meeting of the GST Council (PIB press release, 3 Sep 2025) and FAQs on the decisions of the 56th GST Council
publisher: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Finance, Government of India

title: GST registration threshold limits (goods, services, special category states)
text: Under section 22 of the CGST Act, a supplier must register for GST when aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds Rs 20 lakh (Rs 10 lakh in special category states). Using the power to raise this for suppliers dealing exclusively in goods, Notification 10/2019-Central Tax raised the limit for goods-only suppliers to Rs 40 lakh from 1 April 2019. The Rs 40 lakh option does not apply in Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Puducherry, Sikkim, Telangana, Tripura and Uttarakhand, nor to sellers of ice cream, pan masala or tobacco. In summary: goods-only suppliers Rs 40 lakh in most states (Rs 20 lakh in the listed states, Rs 10 lakh in Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura); service providers, including freelancers, Rs 20 lakh (Rs 10 lakh in Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura). The 56th GST Council FAQ (September 2025) confirmed these thresholds did not change under GST 2.0.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 2(6), 22, 24, 25; CGST Rules 8, 9, 14A; Notification 10/2019-CT; Notification 10/2017-IT; PIB release on 56th GST Council (trade facilitation)

title: What counts in "aggregate turnover" for the GST threshold
text: Aggregate turnover under section 2(6) of the CGST Act is the total value of all taxable supplies, exempt supplies, exports of goods or services and inter-state supplies made by persons having the same PAN, computed on an all-India basis. It excludes GST itself (CGST, SGST, UTGST, IGST and cess) and the value of inward supplies on which you pay tax under reverse charge. Section 22 adds that supplies made on behalf of principals are included. So a shopkeeper with two shops in different states under one PAN must add both shops' sales, and exempt sales such as fresh vegetables also count towards the limit, even though a person dealing only in exempt supplies need not register.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 2(6), 22, 24, 25; CGST Rules 8, 9, 14A; Notification 10/2019-CT; Notification 10/2017-IT; PIB release on 56th GST Council (trade facilitation)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Compulsory GST registration irrespective of turnover
text: Section 24 of the CGST Act requires certain persons to register even if turnover is below the threshold. These include persons making inter-state taxable supplies; casual taxable persons; persons liable to pay tax under reverse charge; non-resident taxable persons; persons required to deduct TDS under section 51; agents supplying on behalf of other taxable persons; input service distributors; persons supplying goods or services through an e-commerce operator that collects TCS under section 52; every such e-commerce operator; and suppliers of online information and database access services or online money gaming from outside India to Indian consumers. Two relaxations exist: service providers making inter-state supplies are exempt up to the normal services threshold (Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax), and from 1 October 2023 small goods sellers on e-commerce platforms can sell within their own state without registration, subject to conditions.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 2(6), 22, 24, 25; CGST Rules 8, 9, 14A; Notification 10/2019-CT; Notification 10/2017-IT; PIB release on 56th GST Council (trade facilitation)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: GST registration for freelancers, consultants and content creators
text: Freelancers, consultants, designers, developers, tutors and content creators supply services, so the services threshold applies: registration is required once aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds Rs 20 lakh (Rs 10 lakh in Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura). Billing clients in other states does not by itself force registration for service providers below this limit, because Notification 10/2017-Integrated Tax exempts inter-state service suppliers up to the threshold. Most professional services, such as consulting, software, design and advertising, are taxed at 18%. Income from foreign clients is an export of services, which is zero-rated: once registered, the freelancer can export without paying IGST by filing a Letter of Undertaking (LUT, Form GST RFD-11), but export receipts still count in aggregate turnover. Detailed export and refund questions should be taken to a CA.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 2(6), 22, 24, 25; CGST Rules 8, 9, 14A; Notification 10/2019-CT; Notification 10/2017-IT; PIB release on 56th GST Council (trade facilitation)
publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Voluntary GST registration below the threshold
text: Section 25(3) of the CGST Act lets a person who is not liable to register under section 22 or 24 take GST registration voluntarily. Once registered, all provisions of the Act apply as for any registered person: the business must charge GST on its taxable supplies, issue tax invoices, file returns such as GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B (or CMP-08 and GSTR-4 under composition), and can claim input tax credit on business purchases. Small businesses often register voluntarily because registered B2B buyers prefer suppliers whose invoices give them input tax credit, or because online marketplaces ask for a GSTIN. The downside is the compliance burden and late fees if returns are missed.

title: How to apply for GST registration (Form GST REG-01) and timelines
text: A person who becomes liable to register must apply within 30 days of becoming liable (section 25(1)); casual and non-resident taxable persons must apply at least 5 days before starting business. The application is filed online on the GST portal (gst.gov.in) in Form GST REG-01 using PAN, mobile number and email, with documents such as proof of place of business and bank details, and Aadhaar authentication of the promoter or authorised signatory (rule 8). Under rule 9 the officer must approve within 7 working days if the application is in order. If Aadhaar authentication is not done, or the system or officer flags the case for physical verification, registration is granted within 30 days after verification. If the officer needs clarification, a notice in REG-03 is issued and the applicant replies in REG-04 within 7 working days.

publisher: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, Government of India

title: Simplified GST registration for small and low-risk businesses (Rule 14A) from 1 November 2025
text: The 56th GST Council recommended an optional simplified registration scheme, operational from 1 November 2025 (CGST Rule 14A, notified by Notification 18/2025-Central Tax). An applicant who, on self-assessment, expects output tax on supplies to registered persons (B2B) not to exceed Rs 2.5 lakh per month, including CGST, SGST/UTGST, IGST and cess, can opt for it in Form GST REG-01. Registration is granted automatically and electronically within three working days, subject to Aadhaar authentication. Only one registration per PAN per state is allowed under the scheme, and a person can later withdraw from it. The government said this would cover about 96% of new applicants.

title: GSTR-1: statement of outward supplies and its due dates
text: GSTR-1 is the statement of outward supplies (sales) that every normal registered taxpayer files under section 37 of the CGST Act. It reports invoice-wise B2B sales, consolidated B2C sales, credit and debit notes, exports and an HSN-wise summary; the details flow to buyers' GSTR-2B so they can claim input tax credit. Monthly filers must file GSTR-1 by the 11th of the following month (for example, September 2026 sales by 11 October 2026). Taxpayers in the QRMP scheme file it quarterly by the 13th of the month after the quarter (for example, July to September 2026 by 13 October 2026). Under section 37(5), GSTR-1 cannot be filed after three years from its due date. Composition taxpayers do not file GSTR-1.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 37, 39, 44, 47; CGST Rules 59, 61, 80; GST portal FAQs on GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP; Notifications 19/2021-CT, 7/2023-CT, 15/2025-CT
publisher: Goods and Services Tax Network / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs

title: GSTR-3B: monthly summary return and tax payment
text: GSTR-3B is the summary return under section 39 in which a regular taxpayer declares total outward supplies, input tax credit claimed, and pays the net tax. Monthly filers must file it by the 20th of the following month (rule 61). For QRMP taxpayers it is filed quarterly, by the 22nd of the month after the quarter for principal places of business in Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Goa, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and some UTs, and by the 24th for all other states, such as Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Punjab and West Bengal. A return cannot be filed after three years from its due date (section 39(11)). From the January 2026 tax period the portal also auto-computes interest on late payment in Table 5.1 of GSTR-3B.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 37, 39, 44, 47; CGST Rules 59, 61, 80; GST portal FAQs on GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP; Notifications 19/2021-CT, 7/2023-CT, 15/2025-CT
publisher: Goods and Services Tax Network / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs

title: QRMP scheme: quarterly returns with monthly tax payment
text: The Quarterly Return Monthly Payment (QRMP) scheme lets registered taxpayers with aggregate turnover up to Rs 5 crore in the preceding financial year file GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B quarterly instead of monthly. Tax must still be paid every month: for the first two months of a quarter, tax is paid by the 25th of the next month through challan PMT-06, either by the fixed-sum method (35% of the last quarter's cash tax, generated by the portal) or by self-assessing actual liability. Tax for the third month is paid with the quarterly GSTR-3B. The optional Invoice Furnishing Facility (IFF) lets QRMP taxpayers upload B2B invoices for the first two months by the 13th of the next month, so their buyers can claim ITC earlier. QRMP suits small shopkeepers and freelancers with few B2B invoices.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 37, 39, 44, 47; CGST Rules 59, 61, 80; GST portal FAQs on GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP; Notifications 19/2021-CT, 7/2023-CT, 15/2025-CT
publisher: Goods and Services Tax Network / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs

title: GSTR-9 annual return and the Rs 2 crore exemption
text: GSTR-9 is the annual return under section 44 of the CGST Act and rule 80, due by 31 December after the end of the financial year (for example, FY 2025-26 by 31 December 2026). Taxpayers with aggregate turnover above Rs 5 crore must also file GSTR-9C, a self-certified reconciliation statement. Small taxpayers are exempt: Notification 15/2025-Central Tax (17 September 2025) exempts registered persons whose aggregate turnover in a financial year is up to Rs 2 crore from filing the annual return for FY 2024-25 onwards; similar year-by-year exemptions were given for earlier years. Composition taxpayers file GSTR-4 instead. An annual return cannot be filed more than three years after its due date (section 44(2)).
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 37, 39, 44, 47; CGST Rules 59, 61, 80; GST portal FAQs on GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP; Notifications 19/2021-CT, 7/2023-CT, 15/2025-CT
publisher: Goods and Services Tax Network / Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs

title: Late fees for GSTR-1, GSTR-3B, GSTR-4 and GSTR-9
text: Section 47 of the CGST Act levies a late fee for filing returns after the due date, reduced by notifications following the 43rd GST Council meeting. For GSTR-3B and GSTR-1, the fee is Rs 50 per day (Rs 25 CGST + Rs 25 SGST), or Rs 20 per day for nil returns, capped per return at Rs 500 for nil returns, Rs 2,000 if prior-year turnover is up to Rs 1.5 crore, Rs 5,000 for Rs 1.5-5 crore and Rs 10,000 above Rs 5 crore. For GSTR-4 (composition), the cap is Rs 500 for nil returns and Rs 2,000 otherwise. For GSTR-9, from FY 2022-23 the fee is Rs 50 per day for turnover up to Rs 5 crore and Rs 100 per day for Rs 5-20 crore, capped at 0.04% of state turnover (Notification 7/2023-CT). Interest at 18% a year is separately payable on late tax payment.
source_title: CGST Act, 2017 - Sections 37, 39, 44, 47; CGST Rules 59, 61, 80; GST portal FAQs on GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and QRMP; Notifications 19/2021-CT, 7/2023-CT, 15/2025-CT

title: Income-tax Act, 2025 comes into force on 1 April 2026
text: The Income-tax Act, 2025 (Act 30 of 2025) replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961. Parliament passed the Bill on 12 August 2025 and the President gave assent on 21 August 2025. Save as otherwise provided, the new Act came into force on 1 April 2026, and the 1961 Act stands repealed from that date (subject to the savings clause in section 536). The new Act is much shorter: 536 sections and 16 schedules, against 819 sections and 14 schedules in the 1961 Act. The Income-tax Rules, 2026 were notified on 20 March 2026 to operationalise the new Act, cutting the rules from 511 to 333 and the forms from 399 to 190, and new form numbers apply from 1 April 2026. The Budget 2026-27 changes for the year 2026-27 were made directly in the new Act through the Finance Act, 2026.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Objective and scope of the New Act; CBDT press release on commencement; FAQs on Interplay and Transition
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: "Tax Year" replaces previous year and assessment year (section 3, Income-tax Act 2025)
text: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 the twin concepts of "previous year" (the year income is earned) and "assessment year" (the following year in which it is assessed) are replaced by a single concept, the "tax year", defined in section 3. A tax year is the twelve-month period of the financial year beginning on 1 April. Income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 is therefore "Tax Year 2026-27"; there is no separate "AY 2027-28" label under the new Act. For a newly set-up business or a new source of income, the first tax year runs from the date it starts until the following 31 March. When reading older documents, FY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27 under the 1961 Act is the last year that uses the old terminology.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Objective and scope of the New Act; CBDT press release on commencement; FAQs on Interplay and Transition
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Which Act applies to which income period (section 536 savings)
text: Which law applies depends on when the income was earned, not when the return is filed. Income earned up to 31 March 2026 (FY 2025-26 and earlier years) remains governed by the Income-tax Act, 1961 and is assessed under it (FY 2025-26 = AY 2026-27). Section 536(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 saves the 1961 Act for proceedings relating to years beginning before 1 April 2026, even if those proceedings start after that date. Income earned from 1 April 2026 onwards is governed by the Income-tax Act, 2025, starting with Tax Year 2026-27. For TDS, salary for March 2026 paid on 31 March 2026 falls under section 192 of the 1961 Act, while salary paid on or after 1 April 2026 falls under section 392 of the 2025 Act. So salary earned in February 2026 is taxed under the 1961 Act.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Objective and scope of the New Act; CBDT press release on commencement; FAQs on Interplay and Transition
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Return for FY 2025-26 filed in 2026 uses 1961 Act forms (AY 2026-27)
text: Even though the Income-tax Act, 2025 is in force from 1 April 2026, the income-tax return for FY 2025-26 (assessment year 2026-27), filed during 2026, is filed under section 139 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 using ITR forms prescribed under the 1961 Act and the Income-tax Rules, 1962. CBDT notified all seven ITR forms (ITR-1 to ITR-7), plus ITR-V and ITR-U, for AY 2026-27 around 30–31 March 2026. Deductions for this return are still claimed under the old section numbers such as 80C, 80D and 87A. The first return under the new Act will be for Tax Year 2026-27, to be filed in 2027 under section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 with forms notified under the Income-tax Rules, 2026.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Objective and scope of the New Act; CBDT press release on commencement; FAQs on Interplay and Transition
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Health and Education Cess at 4% on tax plus surcharge
text: Every individual, under both the old and new regimes, pays a Health and Education Cess of 4% on the income tax (after rebate) plus any surcharge. It applied for FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 through the annual Finance Acts, and section 3 of the Finance Act, 2026 continues the 4% cess for Tax Year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Example: if slab tax after rebate is ₹1,12,500 and there is no surcharge, cess is ₹4,500 and total tax is ₹1,17,000. If the rebate brings tax to zero, cess is also zero. Cess is part of the final tax and also has to be covered in advance tax and TDS.
source_title: Health and Education Cess and Surcharge — e-Filing help AY 2026-27; Finance Act 2026 section 3
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Surcharge rates for individuals: 10%, 15%, 25%, 37%
text: Surcharge is an extra levy on income tax for high earners. For individuals: nil up to ₹50 lakh total income; 10% above ₹50 lakh up to ₹1 crore; 15% above ₹1 crore up to ₹2 crore; 25% above ₹2 crore up to ₹5 crore; and above ₹5 crore, 37% under the old regime but capped at 25% under the new regime (section 115BAC / section 202). Surcharge on capital gains under sections 111A, 112 and 112A and on dividend income is capped at 15%. These rates applied in FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 and continue for Tax Year 2026-27 under section 3 of the Finance Act, 2026. Cess of 4% is then charged on tax plus surcharge. Most first-jobbers and freelancers earning below ₹50 lakh pay no surcharge.
source_title: Health and Education Cess and Surcharge — e-Filing help AY 2026-27; Finance Act 2026 section 3
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Marginal relief on surcharge at ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore, ₹2 crore and ₹5 crore
text: Marginal relief prevents a small rise in income from causing a big jump in tax when you cross a surcharge threshold. If total income slightly exceeds ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore, ₹2 crore or ₹5 crore, the tax plus surcharge cannot exceed the tax plus surcharge payable at exactly that threshold by more than the income above the threshold. Example: at ₹50,10,000, the extra tax caused by the 10% surcharge is limited to ₹10,000 more than the tax on ₹50 lakh. This is different from the rebate marginal relief at ₹12 lakh (new regime), which works under section 87A / section 156. The Finance Act, 2026 contains the same relief formula for Tax Year 2026-27.
source_title: Health and Education Cess and Surcharge — e-Filing help AY 2026-27; Finance Act 2026 section 3
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 80C (now section 123): up to ₹1.5 lakh for PPF, ELSS, LIC, EPF, tuition fees, home-loan principal
text: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allows an individual or HUF to deduct up to ₹1,50,000 a year for specified savings and payments: employee provident fund (EPF) contribution, Public Provident Fund (PPF), ELSS mutual funds, life insurance premium, National Savings Certificate, 5-year tax-saving fixed deposit, Sukanya Samriddhi, children's tuition fees and principal repayment of a home loan. The ₹1.5 lakh cap is shared with 80CCC and 80CCD(1). From Tax Year 2026-27 the same deduction continues as section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the eligible items listed in Schedule XV and the same ₹1,50,000 limit. It is available only under the old regime; the new regime (section 115BAC / section 202) does not allow it.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Extra ₹50,000 for your own NPS contribution — section 80CCD(1B) (section 124)
text: Over and above the ₹1.5 lakh limit of section 80C, section 80CCD(1B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allows an additional deduction of up to ₹50,000 for your own contribution to the National Pension System (NPS). This means a person in the old regime can claim up to ₹2,00,000 in total through 80C plus NPS. The provision continues within section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (pension scheme of the Central Government) from Tax Year 2026-27. It is an old-regime-only benefit: under the new regime your own NPS contribution is not deductible, though the employer's contribution is.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Employer's NPS contribution — section 80CCD(2), allowed in the new regime too
text: If your employer contributes to your NPS account, that amount is first added to your salary and then deducted under section 80CCD(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (section 124(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27). It is one of the few deductions allowed under the new regime. Limits: under the new regime, up to 14% of salary (basic plus DA) for all employers, private or government; under the old regime, 14% for Central or State Government employers and 10% for others. This deduction is outside the ₹1.5 lakh cap of section 80C. Asking the employer to restructure part of CTC as NPS is a common way to save tax in the new regime.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Health insurance premium — section 80D (section 126): ₹25,000 / ₹50,000
text: Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (section 126 of the Income-tax Act, 2025) gives a deduction for medical insurance premium. For yourself, spouse and dependent children the limit is ₹25,000 a year, or ₹50,000 if any of them is a senior citizen. A separate limit of ₹25,000 (₹50,000 if they are senior citizens) applies to premium for parents. Preventive health check-ups up to ₹5,000 are included within these limits, and premium must be paid by a mode other than cash (check-ups can be paid in cash). So a young employee paying for self and senior-citizen parents can claim up to ₹75,000. It is allowed only under the old regime.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Interest on savings and deposits — sections 80TTA and 80TTB (section 153)
text: Section 80TTA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 lets an individual below 60 deduct up to ₹10,000 of interest from savings bank accounts (not fixed deposits). Resident senior citizens instead use section 80TTB, which allows up to ₹50,000 of interest from savings accounts, fixed deposits and post-office deposits; a senior who claims 80TTB cannot also claim 80TTA. In the Income-tax Act, 2025 both are merged into section 153 (interest on deposits) from Tax Year 2026-27, with the same limits. Both are available only under the old regime. Interest itself is taxable as "income from other sources" and must be reported.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Home-loan interest — section 24(b) (section 22): up to ₹2 lakh for a self-occupied house
text: Under section 24(b) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (section 22 of the Income-tax Act, 2025), interest on a loan taken to buy or build a self-occupied house is deductible up to ₹2,00,000 a year (₹30,000 if the loan is for repairs or taken before 1 April 1999), with construction to be completed within five years. This is allowed only under the old regime. For a let-out property, interest is deductible without limit in both regimes, but under the old regime the house-property loss that can be set off against salary is capped at ₹2,00,000, with the balance carried forward for 8 years; under the new regime the loss cannot be set off at all. Principal repayment falls under section 80C, not 24(b).
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: HRA exemption under section 10(13A) — FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26
text: A salaried employee who lives in rented accommodation can exempt part of house rent allowance under section 10(13A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 2A. The exempt amount is the least of: (a) actual HRA received; (b) 50% of salary if the house is in Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi or Chennai, or 40% elsewhere; (c) rent paid minus 10% of salary. "Salary" here means basic plus dearness allowance (if part of retirement benefits) plus turnover-based commission. Example: basic ₹6 lakh, HRA ₹2.4 lakh, rent ₹2.4 lakh in Pune → least of 2.4L, 2.4L (40%) and 1.8L = ₹1,80,000 exempt. If annual rent exceeds ₹1 lakh you must give the landlord's PAN. HRA exemption is available only under the old regime; for FY 2025-26 returns, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad are still non-metro (40%).
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: HRA exemption from Tax Year 2026-27 — eight metro cities at 50%
text: From Tax Year 2026-27, the HRA exemption continues under the Income-tax Act, 2025 as an exemption listed in Schedule III (the corresponding provision of section 10(13A) of the 1961 Act), with the calculation rules in the Income-tax Rules, 2026. The formula is unchanged — least of actual HRA, rent paid minus 10% of salary, and 50% (metro) or 40% (non-metro) of salary — but the Rules 2026 reportedly expand the 50% metro list from four cities (Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai) to eight, adding Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad. Employees must also disclose their relationship with the landlord in the employer declaration form. HRA remains unavailable under the new regime of section 202.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Education-loan interest — section 80E (section 129)
text: Section 80E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (section 129 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27) allows an individual to deduct the entire interest paid on a loan taken from a bank or approved institution for higher education of self, spouse, children or a student for whom the individual is legal guardian. There is no upper monetary limit, but only interest (not principal) qualifies, and the deduction is available for the year repayment of interest starts plus the next seven years — eight years in total. It is useful for first-jobbers repaying a student loan, but it is allowed only under the old regime.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Donations — section 80G (section 133)
text: Section 80G of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (section 133 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27) gives a deduction for donations to approved funds and charitable institutions. Depending on the recipient, the deduction is 100% or 50% of the donation, and for some institutions it is limited to 10% of adjusted gross total income. Donations to funds such as the PM National Relief Fund qualify at 100% without limit. Cash donations above ₹2,000 are not deductible, and the donee's details from Form 10BE should match the return. The deduction is available only under the old regime.
source_title: Deductions under the Income-tax Act — e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2026-27"; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 123, 124, 126, 153 and Schedule XV
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR due dates for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), filed in 2026
text: For income of FY 2025-26 (assessment year 2026-27), returns are filed in 2026 under section 139(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Due dates: 31 July 2026 for salaried individuals, pensioners and others without business income (ITR-1 and ITR-2); 31 August 2026 for business or professional taxpayers whose accounts need no audit, including freelancers filing ITR-3 or ITR-4 under 44ADA — a new date announced in Budget 2026 (earlier 31 July); 31 October 2026 for tax-audit cases, which CBDT extended to 21 November 2026 (with the audit report date moved from 30 September to 21 October 2026); and 30 November 2026 for transfer-pricing cases. Filing on time is needed to choose the old regime if you have business income and to carry forward most losses.
source_title: Return due dates, belated and revised returns, late fees — e-Filing FAQs AY 2026-27; Budget Speech 2026-27; Finance Act 2026; CBDT due-date extension AY 2026-27
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Belated return, revised return and late fees for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)
text: If you miss the due date for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), you can file a belated return under section 139(4) up to 31 December 2026, paying a late fee under section 234F of ₹5,000 (₹1,000 if total income is up to ₹5 lakh) plus interest under section 234A on unpaid tax. To correct a mistake you can file a revised return under section 139(5). From AY 2026-27 the revised-return window is extended to 31 March 2027 (12 months from the end of the financial year, instead of 31 December). A revision filed after 31 December 2026 attracts a fee under section 234I: ₹1,000 if total income is up to ₹5 lakh, ₹5,000 otherwise. An updated return (ITR-U) can be filed later, up to 48 months from the end of the assessment year, with additional tax.
source_title: Return due dates, belated and revised returns, late fees — e-Filing FAQs AY 2026-27; Budget Speech 2026-27; Finance Act 2026; CBDT due-date extension AY 2026-27
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Return due dates for Tax Year 2026-27 under section 263 (filed in 2027)
text: For Tax Year 2026-27, the first year under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the return of income under section 263(1) is due on: 31 July 2027 for salaried individuals and others without business income (the ITR-1/ITR-2 type cases); 31 August 2027 for persons with business or professional income whose accounts are not required to be audited, such as most freelancers on presumptive taxation, and partners of such firms; 31 October 2027 for companies and audit cases; and 30 November 2027 for transfer-pricing cases. The 31 August date for non-audit business cases was introduced by the Finance Act, 2026 (Budget 2026-27). CBDT can extend these dates by notification. A business taxpayer who wants the old regime must exercise the section 202(4) option by the section 263(1) due date.
source_title: Return due dates, belated and revised returns, late fees — e-Filing FAQs AY 2026-27; Budget Speech 2026-27; Finance Act 2026; CBDT due-date extension AY 2026-27
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Belated and revised returns and late fee (section 428) for Tax Year 2026-27
text: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, a belated return for Tax Year 2026-27 under section 263(4) can be filed within nine months from the end of the tax year (by 31 December 2027) or before assessment is completed, whichever is earlier. A revised return under section 263(5) can be filed within twelve months from the end of the tax year (by 31 March 2028), as extended by the Finance Act, 2026. Section 428 replaces section 234F of the 1961 Act: the fee for a late return is ₹1,000 if total income does not exceed ₹5 lakh and ₹5,000 otherwise, and section 428(b) charges the same ₹1,000/₹5,000 for a revised return filed after nine months from the end of the tax year. Interest on unpaid tax is extra.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Presumptive taxation for professionals — section 44ADA (FY 2024-25, FY 2025-26)
text: Under section 44ADA of the Income-tax Act, 1961, a resident individual or partnership firm (not an LLP) in a specified profession — such as software or IT consulting treated as technical consultancy, engineering, architecture, medicine, law, accountancy, interior decoration or film artists — can declare 50% of gross receipts as taxable profit without keeping detailed books. The scheme is available if gross receipts do not exceed ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh where cash receipts are not more than 5% of total receipts. You can declare more than 50% but not less (unless you keep books and get an audit). No separate deduction for expenses is allowed beyond the 50% assumption. The return is filed in ITR-4 by 31 August 2026 for FY 2025-26.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Presumptive taxation for small businesses — section 44AD: 8% or 6% of turnover
text: Section 44AD of the Income-tax Act, 1961 lets a resident individual, HUF or firm (not an LLP) running an eligible business declare profit at 8% of turnover, or 6% of turnover received through banking channels or digital modes. It is available if turnover does not exceed ₹2 crore, or ₹3 crore where cash receipts are not more than 5% of turnover. It does not cover professionals under section 44AA (they use 44ADA), commission or brokerage income, or agency business. If a person opts out of 44AD after using it, they cannot come back for the next five years. Returns are filed in ITR-4; there is no requirement to maintain books of account.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 — presumptive taxation from Tax Year 2026-27
text: From Tax Year 2026-27, sections 44AD, 44ADA and 44AE of the 1961 Act are consolidated into a single section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in a table format. The core rules carry over: eligible professionals declare 50% of gross receipts as profit (receipts up to ₹50 lakh, or ₹75 lakh if cash receipts are within 5%); eligible small businesses declare 8% of turnover, or 6% of digital/banking receipts (turnover up to ₹2 crore, or ₹3 crore if cash is within 5%); and goods-carriage owners with up to ten vehicles use per-vehicle income. Commentators note some tightening, such as stricter disqualification for minor commission income and a full bar on setting off losses against presumptive income. The tax-audit provision (old section 44AB) corresponds to section 63.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Advance tax: ₹10,000 threshold and 15/45/75/100% instalments
text: If your tax liability for the year, after subtracting TDS and TCS, is ₹10,000 or more, you must pay advance tax during the year itself — section 208 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, continued as section 404 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The cumulative instalments are: at least 15% by 15 June, 45% by 15 September, 75% by 15 December and 100% by 15 March. A resident senior citizen (60+) with no business or professional income is exempt from advance tax. Salaried employees usually need not pay it because the employer deducts TDS, but a salaried person with large interest, capital gains or freelance income on the side may have to. Pay online through the e-filing portal using challan ITNS 280.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Advance tax for presumptive taxpayers and interest for late payment
text: Freelancers and businesses using presumptive taxation (section 44AD or 44ADA, now section 58) need not pay four instalments: they can pay 100% of their advance tax in a single instalment on or before 15 March of the year. If advance tax is not paid or is short, interest is charged: under section 234B (section 424 of the Income-tax Act, 2025), simple interest of 1% per month if advance tax paid is less than 90% of the assessed tax; and under section 234C, 1% per month for deferment of individual instalments (for presumptive taxpayers, only for a shortfall at 15 March). Example: a freelancer with ₹30 lakh receipts under 44ADA declares ₹15 lakh profit and should pay the full advance tax by 15 March.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: TDS on freelance professional fees — section 194J (section 393)
text: When a business or professional client pays a resident freelancer fees for professional services, it must deduct TDS under section 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 — 10% for professional fees and royalty, 2% for fees for technical services and certain other payments — once payments to that person cross ₹50,000 in a financial year (threshold raised from ₹30,000 by the Finance Act, 2025, from 1 April 2025). Contract work falls under section 194C instead (1% individuals, 2% others). From 1 April 2026 these TDS provisions (192 to 194T) are consolidated into sections 392 (salary) and 393 (other payments) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with similar rates. If you do not give your PAN, TDS is deducted at a higher rate of 20%. TDS is only a prepayment; it is adjusted against your final tax.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Form 26AS and the Annual Information Statement (AIS)
text: Form 26AS is your annual tax credit statement on the e-filing portal: it shows TDS and TCS deducted against your PAN, advance tax and self-assessment tax you paid, and refunds. The Annual Information Statement (AIS) is a wider report showing income and transactions reported by banks, employers, mutual funds and others — salary, interest, dividends, securities sales, rent and high-value transactions — with a simplified Taxpayer Information Summary (TIS). Before filing, freelancers should match their gross receipts and TDS with 26AS/AIS, because the department compares the return with this data and mismatches can lead to notices. You can give feedback in AIS if any entry is wrong.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Form 16 — the TDS certificate for salaried employees
text: Form 16 is the certificate an employer issues for tax deducted from salary under section 192 of the Income-tax Act, 1961; it must be issued by 15 June after the end of the financial year. Part A shows TAN, PAN and quarterly TDS deposited; Part B shows the salary break-up, exemptions such as HRA, the standard deduction, Chapter VI-A deductions, the regime chosen and the tax computed. A freelancer paid professional fees instead receives Form 16A, a quarterly TDS certificate from each client. From 1 April 2026 salary TDS is governed by section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, and the certificate has a new number under the Income-tax Rules, 2026; the content remains similar. For FY 2025-26 salaries, Form 16 is issued under the 1961 Act.
source_title: Presumptive taxation, advance tax and TDS for freelancers — e-Filing ITR-4 FAQs; Income-tax Act 2025 sections 58, 392, 393, 404, 424
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR-1 (Sahaj) eligibility for AY 2026-27 (FY 2025-26)
text: ITR-1 (Sahaj) is the simplest return, for a resident (ordinarily resident) individual with total income up to ₹50 lakh from salary or pension, up to two house properties (raised from one property for AY 2026-27), other sources such as interest, agricultural income up to ₹5,000, and long-term capital gains under section 112A (listed shares/equity funds) up to ₹1.25 lakh. You cannot use ITR-1 if you have business or professional income, any short-term capital gains, LTCG above ₹1.25 lakh, are a company director, held unlisted equity shares, have foreign assets or foreign income, or have losses to carry forward. A typical first-job salaried employee with salary, a savings account and an FD files ITR-1. Due date: 31 July 2026.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR-2 for individuals with capital gains or other complex non-business income (AY 2026-27)
text: ITR-2 is for individuals and HUFs who do not have income from business or profession but cannot use ITR-1 — for example, total income above ₹50 lakh, short-term capital gains or LTCG above ₹1.25 lakh from shares or mutual funds, sale of property, more than two house properties, foreign assets or income, being a company director, holding unlisted shares, or losses to carry forward. Non-residents and RNORs with salary also use ITR-2. Its due date for AY 2026-27 is 31 July 2026, the same as ITR-1. A salaried person who sold mutual funds at a short-term gain during FY 2025-26 must therefore switch from ITR-1 to ITR-2.
