publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR-3 for freelancers and professionals with regular books (AY 2026-27)
text: ITR-3 is for individuals and HUFs having income from business or profession that is not declared on a presumptive basis, or who otherwise cannot use ITR-4 — for example, a freelancer who keeps books and declares actual profit, who has capital gains along with business income, is a partner in a firm, trades in futures and options, or has income above ₹50 lakh. It covers salary, house property, capital gains and other income as well. For AY 2026-27 the due date is 31 August 2026 if no tax audit is required, and the audit-case date (31 October 2026, extended by CBDT to 21 November 2026) if accounts must be audited under section 44AB.
source_title: e-Filing FAQs — ITR-1 (Sahaj), ITR-4 (Sugam) for AY 2026-27; Income-tax (Amendment) Rules 2026 notifying ITR forms
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR-4 (Sugam) for presumptive income under 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE (AY 2026-27)
text: ITR-4 (Sugam) is for a resident individual, HUF or firm (other than an LLP) with total income up to ₹50 lakh that includes business or professional income computed on a presumptive basis under section 44AD (business), 44ADA (specified professionals such as software consultants, doctors, designers) or 44AE (up to ten goods carriages). It can also include salary, up to two house properties, interest, agricultural income up to ₹5,000 and LTCG under section 112A up to ₹1.25 lakh. It cannot be used with short-term capital gains, income above ₹50 lakh, or as a company director. The due date for AY 2026-27 is 31 August 2026. A freelancer wanting the old regime must file Form 10-IEA before that date.
source_title: e-Filing FAQs — ITR-1 (Sahaj), ITR-4 (Sugam) for AY 2026-27; Income-tax (Amendment) Rules 2026 notifying ITR forms
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: ITR forms for Tax Year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025
text: Returns for Tax Year 2026-27, the first year under the Income-tax Act, 2025, will be filed in 2027 under section 263 using return forms prescribed under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. As of October 2026 the new return forms for Tax Year 2026-27 are expected to be notified before 1 April 2027. The Income-tax Rules, 2026 renumbered almost all forms, so the return forms may carry new names or numbers instead of the familiar ITR-1 to ITR-7; check the final form names and eligibility limits on the e-filing portal once notified. Until then, the AY 2026-27 rules — ₹50 lakh income cap for ITR-1/ITR-4, LTCG under section 112A (now the corresponding capital-gains section of the 2025 Act) up to ₹1.25 lakh — are the best guide.
source_title: e-Filing FAQs — ITR-1 (Sahaj), ITR-4 (Sugam) for AY 2026-27; Income-tax (Amendment) Rules 2026 notifying ITR forms
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 80C (1961) = Section 123 (2025 Act); 80CCC/80CCD = Section 124
text: Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Yes, the 80C deduction still exists from Tax Year 2026-27, only under a new number: section 123 allows up to ₹1,50,000 for the payments listed in Schedule XV (PF, PPF, life insurance, ELSS, tuition fees, home-loan principal and so on). The pension deductions of sections 80CCC and 80CCD of the 1961 Act — including 80CCD(1B) self NPS and 80CCD(2) employer NPS — correspond to section 124 of the 2025 Act. Chapter VI-A of the 1961 Act (sections 80A to 80U) as a whole becomes Chapter VIII of the 2025 Act, roughly sections 123 to 154. For FY 2025-26 returns filed in 2026, you still quote section 80C.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 80D = 126, 80E = 129, 80G = 133, 80GG = 134
text: Health-insurance deduction: Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 126 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Education-loan interest: Section 80E of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 129 of the 2025 Act. Donations: Section 80G of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 133 of the 2025 Act. Rent paid by people who get no HRA: Section 80GG of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 134 of the 2025 Act. Person with disability: Section 80U corresponds to Section 154. The amounts and conditions are carried over; what changes from Tax Year 2026-27 is the section number you cite. All of these are available only if you opt out of the new regime of section 202.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Sections 80TTA and 80TTB (1961) = Section 153 (2025 Act)
text: Section 80TTA (savings-account interest up to ₹10,000) and Section 80TTB (deposit interest up to ₹50,000 for resident senior citizens) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 are merged into a single Section 153 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, titled deduction in respect of interest on deposits. The limits are unchanged from Tax Year 2026-27. As before, a senior citizen gets the higher ₹50,000 limit covering fixed deposits too, and others get ₹10,000 on savings interest only. Section 153 is not available in the default new regime of section 202.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 87A (1961) = Section 156; Section 115BAC = Section 202
text: The rebate of section 87A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (₹12,500 up to ₹5 lakh in section 156(1); ₹60,000 up to ₹12 lakh for the new regime in section 156(2), with marginal relief). The new tax regime of section 115BAC of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025; the slabs are now written into section 202(1) itself. Relief under section 89 for salary arrears corresponds to section 157 of the 2025 Act. So "87A rebate" in FY 2025-26 language means the "section 156 rebate" from Tax Year 2026-27.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 16 = Section 19; Section 24(b) = Section 22; HRA 10(13A) = Schedule III
text: Deductions from salary in Section 16 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (including the standard deduction in 16(ia)) correspond to Section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Deductions from house-property income in Section 24 of the 1961 Act, including the ₹2 lakh home-loan interest limit of 24(b), correspond to Section 22 of the 2025 Act. The exemptions of section 10 of the 1961 Act were moved into Schedules of the 2025 Act; the HRA exemption of section 10(13A) corresponds to an entry in Schedule III (exempt allowances), with the formula in the Income-tax Rules, 2026. Exact Schedule serial numbers were not confirmed from an official mapping table.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Sections 44AD, 44ADA, 44AE = Section 58; 44AB tax audit = Section 63
text: The three presumptive-taxation provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 44AD (small business, 8%/6% of turnover), Section 44ADA (professionals, 50% of receipts) and Section 44AE (goods carriages) — are consolidated into a single Section 58 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which sets them out in one table. Tax audit under Section 44AB of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 63 of the 2025 Act (this pairing is from secondary sources). A freelancer who used 44ADA for FY 2025-26 will use section 58 for Tax Year 2026-27.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 139 = Section 263 (return of income); 234F = Section 428
text: Filing of the return of income under Section 139 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 2025: 139(1) original return due dates → 263(1), 139(4) belated return → 263(4), 139(5) revised return → 263(5). The late-filing fee of Section 234F of the 1961 Act corresponds to Section 428 of the 2025 Act, which also absorbs the fee for late revised returns (old section 234I). Section 427 corresponds to the fee for late TDS/TCS statements (old section 234E). The Finance Act, 2026 substituted sections 427 and 428 to consolidate these fees.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: TDS sections 192 to 194T = Sections 392 and 393
text: All TDS provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (sections 192 to 194T) are consolidated in the Income-tax Act, 2025: TDS on salary under Section 192 corresponds to Section 392, and TDS on other payments — contractors (194C), professional and technical fees (194J), interest (194A), rent (194I), and so on — corresponds to Section 393, which lists them in tables. Section 197A (Form 15G/15H declarations) corresponds to section 393(6). The higher TDS rate when the payee has no PAN (old section 206AA) has a corresponding provision in the 2025 Act; secondary sources cite section 397, but this could not be confirmed officially. Payments made from 1 April 2026 follow the new sections.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 143 = Section 270; reassessment 147–153 = Sections 279–286
text: Assessment provisions are renumbered in the Income-tax Act, 2025. Processing and scrutiny assessment under Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 corresponds to Section 270 of the 2025 Act. The income-escaping-assessment provisions, sections 147 to 153 of the 1961 Act (including the notice under section 148), correspond to sections 279 to 286 of the 2025 Act, with section 148 reported as section 280. Notices for FY 2025-26 and earlier years can still be issued under the 1961 Act because of the savings clause in section 536 of the 2025 Act.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Advance tax: Section 208 = 404, 211 = 408; interest 234B = 424; previous year = tax year (s.3)
text: The obligation to pay advance tax when liability is ₹10,000 or more, Section 208 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, corresponds to Section 404 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The instalment schedule of Section 211 (15 June, 15 September, 15 December, 15 March) corresponds to Section 408 of the 2025 Act, and the exemption for resident senior citizens without business income (old section 207) continues. Interest for default in advance tax under Section 234B corresponds to Section 424. Finally, the "previous year" of section 3 and the "assessment year" of section 2(9) of the 1961 Act are replaced by the single "tax year" defined in Section 3 of the 2025 Act.
source_title: Section mapping — Income-tax Act, 1961 to Income-tax Act, 2025 (e-Filing "Objective and scope of the New Act"; CBDT FAQs on Interplay and Transition; secondary comparison tables)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: New tax regime slabs under section 115BAC for FY 2024-25 (AY 2025-26)
text: For FY 2024-25 (assessment year 2025-26), the default new tax regime under section 115BAC(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 had these slabs for individuals of every age: income up to ₹3,00,000 – nil; ₹3,00,001 to ₹7,00,000 – 5%; ₹7,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 – 10%; ₹10,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 – 15%; ₹12,00,001 to ₹15,00,000 – 20%; above ₹15,00,000 – 30%. In cumulative terms, tax is ₹20,000 at ₹7 lakh, ₹50,000 at ₹10 lakh, ₹80,000 at ₹12 lakh and ₹1,40,000 at ₹15 lakh. Salaried taxpayers got a standard deduction of ₹75,000 under this regime for FY 2024-25. Health and education cess of 4% is added. These slabs were replaced from FY 2025-26 by the Finance Act, 2025.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 87A rebate under the new regime for FY 2024-25: ₹25,000 up to ₹7 lakh
text: For FY 2024-25 (AY 2025-26), a resident individual taxed under the new regime of section 115BAC(1A) could claim a rebate under section 87A of up to ₹25,000 if total income did not exceed ₹7,00,000. Since slab tax on exactly ₹7 lakh is ₹20,000, the rebate in practice wiped out the whole tax up to ₹7 lakh of taxable income (about ₹7.75 lakh salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction). Marginal relief applied just above ₹7 lakh: the tax payable could not exceed the amount by which total income exceeded ₹7,00,000. Example: taxable income ₹7,15,000 gives slab tax ₹21,500, but tax is limited to ₹15,000. Non-residents cannot claim the rebate. Some e-filing pages show "₹20,000" for this year, which reflects the tax at ₹7 lakh, not the statutory cap.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: New tax regime slabs under section 115BAC for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)
text: For FY 2025-26 (assessment year 2026-27), the Finance Act, 2025 revised the new-regime slabs in section 115BAC(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961: income up to ₹4,00,000 – nil; ₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 – 5%; ₹8,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 – 10%; ₹12,00,001 to ₹16,00,000 – 15%; ₹16,00,001 to ₹20,00,000 – 20%; ₹20,00,001 to ₹24,00,000 – 25%; above ₹24,00,000 – 30%. The same slabs apply to all ages, including senior citizens. Cumulative tax is ₹20,000 at ₹8 lakh, ₹60,000 at ₹12 lakh, ₹1,20,000 at ₹16 lakh, ₹2,00,000 at ₹20 lakh and ₹3,00,000 at ₹24 lakh, before 4% cess. The standard deduction for salaried employees stays at ₹75,000. This is the regime that applies to the return filed in 2026.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"

title: Section 87A rebate up to ₹60,000 and marginal relief for FY 2025-26
text: For FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), a resident individual under the new regime of section 115BAC(1A) gets a rebate under section 87A of up to ₹60,000 if total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000. Because slab tax at ₹12 lakh is exactly ₹60,000, there is no income tax up to ₹12 lakh of taxable income, which for a salaried person means about ₹12.75 lakh of salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction. Marginal relief applies just above ₹12 lakh: tax cannot exceed the income above ₹12,00,000. Example: taxable income ₹12,25,000 gives slab tax ₹63,750 but tax is limited to ₹25,000 (₹26,000 with 4% cess). The rebate does not apply to income taxed at special rates, such as capital gains under sections 111A and 112A. Under the old regime the rebate is only ₹12,500 up to ₹5 lakh.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Standard deduction under section 16(ia): ₹75,000 new regime, ₹50,000 old regime (FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26)
text: Under section 16(ia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, every salaried employee and pensioner gets a flat standard deduction from salary income without any bills or proof. For FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26, it is ₹75,000 or the amount of salary, whichever is lower, if you are taxed under the new regime of section 115BAC(1A), and ₹50,000 or the salary, whichever is lower, under the old regime. Freelancers and consultants who earn professional fees, not salary, do not get the standard deduction. The same amounts continue under section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Deductions allowed and not allowed under the new regime (section 115BAC)
text: Under the new regime of section 115BAC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26), most exemptions and Chapter VI-A deductions are not allowed. You cannot claim section 80C (PPF, ELSS, LIC, EPF), 80CCD(1B) self NPS, 80D health insurance, 80E, 80G, 80TTA/80TTB, the HRA exemption under section 10(13A), LTA, or interest on a self-occupied home loan under section 24(b). What is still allowed: the ₹75,000 standard deduction, the employer's contribution to NPS under section 80CCD(2) up to 14% of salary for all employers, the Agniveer Corpus Fund deduction under section 80CCH, and interest on a let-out house property (but its loss cannot be set off against other income). The trade-off is the lower slab rates and the bigger rebate.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: New regime is the default; how to opt for the old regime (section 115BAC(6))
text: Since AY 2024-25 the new regime under section 115BAC is the default for individuals. A salaried person or anyone without business or professional income can choose the old regime afresh every year, simply by selecting it in the return (ITR-1 or ITR-2) filed by the due date under section 139(1); no separate form is needed. The employer may deduct TDS based on the regime you declare during the year, but the final choice is made in the return. A person with business or professional income (ITR-3/ITR-4) who wants the old regime must file Form 10-IEA on or before the section 139(1) due date. Such a person can switch back to the new regime only once in a lifetime.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 1961 — Section 115BAC (new tax regime) and Section 87A; e-Filing help "Salaried Individuals for AY 2025-26 / AY 2026-27"

title: Section 202 — New tax regime slab rates for Tax Year 2026-27
text: Section 202(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (which replaces section 115BAC of the 1961 Act) sets the default new-regime rates for individuals, HUFs, AOPs, BOIs and artificial juridical persons from Tax Year 2026-27: total income up to ₹4,00,000 – nil; ₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 – 5%; ₹8,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 – 10%; ₹12,00,001 to ₹16,00,000 – 15%; ₹16,00,001 to ₹20,00,000 – 20%; ₹20,00,001 to ₹24,00,000 – 25%; above ₹24,00,000 – 30%. The rates are the same as for FY 2025-26; Budget 2026 did not change the slabs. Unlike the 1961 Act, the slabs are written into the Act itself. The same rates apply to senior and super-senior citizens. A 4% health and education cess is added on tax plus surcharge.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 156 — rebate up to ₹60,000 if total income is up to ₹12 lakh (Tax Year 2026-27)
text: Section 156 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces section 87A of the 1961 Act. Under section 156(2), a resident individual taxed under the new regime of section 202(1) gets a rebate equal to 100% of tax or ₹60,000, whichever is less, if total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000. So there is effectively no tax up to ₹12 lakh of taxable income (₹12.75 lakh of salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction). For income above ₹12 lakh, marginal relief applies: the tax payable cannot exceed the amount by which total income exceeds ₹12,00,000. Section 156(1) keeps the old-regime rebate of up to ₹12,500 for total income up to ₹5,00,000. Only resident individuals qualify; HUFs, firms and non-residents do not.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Why "no tax up to ₹12 lakh" and "5% from ₹4 lakh" are both true (new regime, FY 2025-26 and Tax Year 2026-27)
text: Many taxpayers are confused because the new-regime slab table charges 5% from ₹4 lakh, yet people say income up to ₹12 lakh is tax-free. Both are true. First, tax is worked out on the slabs: 5% on ₹4–8 lakh (₹20,000) and 10% on ₹8–12 lakh (₹40,000), so ₹60,000 at ₹12 lakh of taxable income. Then the rebate (section 87A of the 1961 Act for FY 2025-26, section 156 of the 2025 Act from Tax Year 2026-27) cancels tax of up to ₹60,000 for a resident individual whose total income is not more than ₹12 lakh, so the tax becomes nil. For a salaried person the ₹75,000 standard deduction makes this about ₹12.75 lakh of salary. Above ₹12 lakh the rebate is lost and every slab is taxed, not only the part above ₹12 lakh: at ₹16 lakh taxable income tax is ₹1,20,000 plus 4% cess. Just above ₹12 lakh, marginal relief caps the tax at the income above ₹12 lakh.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

Step 2, the rebate: section 156 (section 87A of the old Act) cancels up to ₹60,000 of tax for a resident individual whose total income is not more than ₹12 lakh, so the tax you actually pay is nil. Above ₹12 lakh the rebate is lost and every slab is taxed (at ₹16 lakh: ₹1,20,000 plus 4% cess), with marginal relief easing the jump just above ₹12 lakh.

title: Section 19 — standard deduction ₹75,000 (new regime) or ₹50,000 (old regime) from Tax Year 2026-27
text: Section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 lists the deductions from salary income and replaces section 16 of the 1961 Act. The standard deduction is ₹75,000 or the amount of salary, whichever is less, where income-tax is computed under the new regime of section 202(1), and ₹50,000 or the salary, whichever is less, in any other case (the old regime). The amounts are unchanged from FY 2025-26. It is available to salaried employees and pensioners automatically, with no proof needed. Self-employed people and freelancers with only business or professional income do not get it.

title: Section 202(2) — exemptions and deductions not allowed in the new regime (Tax Year 2026-27)
text: Under section 202(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, total income in the new regime is computed without most exemptions in Schedule III (such as house rent allowance and leave travel concession) and without the deductions in Chapter VIII, except a few carved out: section 124(1) and 124(2) (pension scheme contributions, including the employer's NPS contribution, the old section 80CCD(2), up to 14% of salary), section 125(2) (Agniveer Corpus Fund) and section 146. So the old 80C (now section 123), 80D (now 126), 80TTA/80TTB (now 153), HRA and self-occupied home-loan interest cannot be claimed. Loss from house property cannot be set off against other heads. The ₹75,000 standard deduction under section 19 remains available.
source_title: Income-tax Act, 2025 — Section 202 (new tax regime), Section 156 (rebate), Section 19 (deductions from salaries), as amended by Finance Act 2026
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Section 202(4) — choosing the old regime from Tax Year 2026-27
text: The new regime of section 202(1) is the default under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Section 202(4) lets a person opt out. Someone without business or professional income (for example a salaried employee) exercises the option along with the return of income under section 263(1) for that tax year, so the choice can be made fresh every year. A person with business or professional income must exercise the option on or before the due date under section 263(1); once exercised it continues for later years and can be withdrawn only once, after which the person can never opt out again unless they stop having business income. The 1961 Act equivalent was section 115BAC(6) with Form 10-IEA; the corresponding form under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 has a new number.

publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Old tax regime slabs for individuals below 60 years
text: Under the old (optional) tax regime, an individual below 60 years pays: income up to ₹2,50,000 – nil; ₹2,50,001 to ₹5,00,000 – 5%; ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 – 20%; above ₹10,00,000 – 30%. Cumulative tax is ₹12,500 at ₹5 lakh and ₹1,12,500 at ₹10 lakh, plus 4% cess. These rates have not changed for many years: they applied for FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and the Finance Act, 2026 keeps the same basic exemption of ₹2,50,000 for Tax Year 2026-27 for people who opt out of section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The old regime allows deductions such as 80C, 80D, HRA and home-loan interest, and a standard deduction of ₹50,000.
source_title: Old tax regime — slab rates, rebate and deductions (Income-tax Act, 1961 Finance Acts; Finance Act 2026 First Schedule for Tax Year 2026-27)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Old regime slabs for senior (60–80) and super-senior (80+) citizens
text: The old regime gives older residents a higher exemption limit. A resident senior citizen aged 60 to below 80 pays nil up to ₹3,00,000, 5% on ₹3,00,001 to ₹5,00,000, 20% on ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 and 30% above ₹10,00,000 (tax ₹10,000 at ₹5 lakh). A resident super-senior citizen aged 80 or more pays nil up to ₹5,00,000, 20% on ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 and 30% above ₹10,00,000. These limits applied in FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26 and continue for Tax Year 2026-27 under the Finance Act, 2026. The new regime has no age-based slabs: its nil band of ₹4 lakh (₹3 lakh in FY 2024-25) is the same for everyone.
source_title: Old tax regime — slab rates, rebate and deductions (Income-tax Act, 1961 Finance Acts; Finance Act 2026 First Schedule for Tax Year 2026-27)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: Old regime rebate: up to ₹12,500 if total income is up to ₹5 lakh
text: A resident individual who chooses the old regime gets a rebate of up to ₹12,500 if total income (after deductions) does not exceed ₹5,00,000 — section 87A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26, and section 156(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from Tax Year 2026-27. Since old-regime tax at ₹5 lakh is exactly ₹12,500 (₹10,000 for seniors), tax becomes zero up to ₹5 lakh taxable income. There is no marginal relief in the old regime: at ₹5,00,001 the full slab tax of about ₹12,500 is payable. Compare the new regime: ₹60,000 up to ₹12 lakh from FY 2025-26, or ₹25,000 up to ₹7 lakh in FY 2024-25.
source_title: Old tax regime — slab rates, rebate and deductions (Income-tax Act, 1961 Finance Acts; Finance Act 2026 First Schedule for Tax Year 2026-27)
publisher: Income Tax Department, Government of India

title: What the old regime allows that the new regime does not
text: The old regime has higher slab rates but lets you reduce taxable income with exemptions and deductions. The main ones for salaried people are: standard deduction ₹50,000; HRA exemption; leave travel allowance; professional tax; section 80C investments up to ₹1,50,000 (section 123 of the 2025 Act); extra NPS contribution under 80CCD(1B) up to ₹50,000; health insurance under 80D (₹25,000, or ₹50,000 for seniors, plus parents); savings interest under 80TTA (₹10,000) or 80TTB for seniors (₹50,000); education-loan interest under 80E; donations under 80G; and up to ₹2,00,000 interest on a self-occupied home loan. As a rule of thumb, the old regime wins only if your total deductions are large — for most salaried people earning up to about ₹12.75 lakh, the new regime gives zero tax from FY 2025-26.
source_title: Old tax regime — slab rates, rebate and deductions (Income-tax Act, 1961 Finance Acts; Finance Act 2026 First Schedule for Tax Year 2026-27)
